summary: This note describes the Allies of World War II, the countries that opposed the Axis powers from 1939 to 1945. It traces how the alliance grew from France, Poland and the United Kingdom at the war's start, through the Dominions, the Low Countries, Greece, Yugoslavia, the Soviet Union, the United States and China. The alliance became known as the United Nations after a 1 January 1942 declaration.
one_line: Overview of the countries that joined the Allies against the Axis powers in World War II, and how the alliance grew from 1939 to 1942.
key_facts: At the start of the war on 1 September 1939, the Allies consisted of France, Poland and the United Kingdom, as well as their dependent states such as British India.
Within days of the war's start, the independent Dominions of the British Commonwealth (Australia, Canada, New Zealand and South Africa) joined the Allies.
After the start of the German invasion of North Europe until the Balkan Campaign, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece and Yugoslavia joined the Allies.
The Soviet Union had first cooperated with Germany in invading Poland while remaining neutral in the Allied-Axis conflict.
The Soviet Union joined the Allies in June 1941 after being invaded by Germany.
The United States provided war materiel and money throughout the war and officially joined in December 1941 after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor.
China had been in a prolonged war with Japan since the Marco Polo Bridge Incident of 1937 and officially joined the Allies in 1941.
The Allies of World War II were called the United Nations from a 1 January 1942 declaration.
The Allies were the countries that together opposed the Axis powers during the Second World War (1939 to 1945).
The Allies promoted the alliance as seeking to stop German, Japanese and Italian aggression.
